Question: Why are there multiple programming languages instead of one dominant language like Python or Java?
Answer: The same reason why there are many kinds of tools: spanners, wrenches, drills, screwdrivers, hammers, pipes, hacksaw blades, etc. Have you ever seen a mechanic who would work with only one tool? Every programming language that has a considerable following, has solved a class of problems that the other, previous languages had been unsuitable for; it's almost a cliche to say that different problems require different tools. Here are some examples of reasons why new languages appear: a clear but non-verbose syntax (Scala for JVM), a more effective and realistic way to deal with complexity without compromising safety and speed (Rust), doing the same things more comfortably and safely, without deviating too much (Go), elegant syntactic sugar for LLVM and a programmer-friendly way to write apps (Swift), quick pseudo-code for glue scripting, which led to a lot of creativity and hence lots of excellent libraries for AI/ML (Python), make programming fun again (Ruby), make fun programming fast and scalable (Elixir, Crystal), make Python faster than C++ (Mojo), make Javascript frameworks obsolete (Blazor), make front-end fun again (Elm, Purescript), make HTML more interesting and powerful (Htmx), make Java suck less (Kotlin), make Javascript safer and saner (Typescript), make functional programming real-world-ready (OCaml), make programming extremely addictive and contribute to its future improvements (Haskell), make a dozen languages [[potentially]] retire (V), make scientific programming easy, fast, fun and free (Julia), when programming meets mathematics: APL, Mathematica..the list is long.

Question: What is it like to be a foreigner living in Beijing?
Answer: I lived in Beijing between 2006 and 2016, so I know what I’m writing about (unlike some of the Quorans here who write based on a two-day experience). Further, my answer is also the most up-to date, as I went back for a short visit last month. Your question is too general, so maybe a book can answer it. But we can summarize: it’s fantastic. Nobody will shout at you just because you don’t speak their language. (No Karens here). Nobody will randomly punch you like they do in NY. Nobody will tell you to ‘go back to where you came from’. Urban Beijingers are a very civilized, highly-educated, interesting, polite, kind, and calm, rational people. In 2000, when I first arrived, Beijing had two subway lines: one red, one blue. By 2004, they had added a yellow line, which covered what was then considered the ‘outskirts’: In 2024? You can go anywhere with the subway. This also means the city has expanded considerably. It also has a second airport in the south: You might enjoy the hutongs (ancient alleys and courtyards) but it also boasts modern architecture. I used to have my lunch here, nearly every day: As you can see, the pollution is gone. For the 30 days I spent in 2024, every single day was clean (it had serious air pollution in 2015 and 2016, which had prompted me to leave). I saw some statistics that confirms my observation. As of 2024, the air pollution problem has been solved. And speaking of food, you can easily find foreign dishes anywhere in the Central Business District (as well as in the southern Chaoyang district in general): Local dishes are better, though, and I recommend them. The very best food in the world, imho, is Chinese. I know this somewhat of a generalization, but just one authentic 干煸豆角 dish will sway your opinion as well： Beijing is also extremely safe. At any time of the night or day. And in any area. However, exercise caution and act rationally just like you would anywhere. So, for instance, don’t go to a ‘lady bah’ when a dodgy-looking man or woman tries to persuade you. I know someone, a Spanish man, who went to one of these ‘lady bars’ and ended up drinking a 200-$ cup of tea. :) So, it’s safe—but not if you create trouble for yourself. Costs? A bit more expensive (and certainly more expensive than Thailand) but this depends on you. One month rent for a one-bedroom studio is between 500US$ to 1000US$ depending on location. One western/foreign meal is around 10$ to 30$, but local dishes start from 5$ and go all the way up to 100$. Typically, though, a local dish costs around 15$. Entertainment? You can hike, swim, dance, skate, go to the opera, etc. etc. There’s the Great Wall, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Fragrant mountains, the Botanical Garden, etc. You will need to bring your own books though, as English books have become rare now; the iconic Foreign Languages bookstore (in Wangfujing) which was among the most favorite and relaxing places for me in Beijing, has closed down. :( However, there’s one foreign language bookstore that still offers books in English: PageONE in Sanlitun area. The selections are limited but it’s better than nothing. But of course, you can also buy some English books online. For instance, I bought Thaler’s “Nudge” at: But this requires fluency in Chinese. You can also ask a Chinese friend to help you buy from this second-hand online bookstore. In short, it’s comfortable and pleasant. Although I no longer live and work in Beijing, I visit at least twice a year.

Question: Why does ['1', '7', '11'].map (parseInt) returns [1, NaN, 3] in Javascript?
Answer: One might expect this to return an array of integers: [1, 7, 11]. Quite annoying, isn't it? parseInt takes two arguments: If the radix is omitted or set to 0, parseInt assumes base 10 (decimal) unless the string starts with "0x" or "0X", in which case it's interpreted as hexadecimal (base 16). The map method calls parseInt for each element in the array, passing the element value as the first argument and the index as the second argument: 1. parseInt('1', 0): Since 1 does not start with "0x" or "0X", the radix is assumed to be 10 (decimal), so parseInt('1', 10) returns 1. 2. parseInt('7', 1): Since the radix is 1 (which is not allowed in JavaScript), parseInt returns NaN. 3. parseInt('11', 2): Since the radix is 2 (binary), parseInt tries to parse ‘11’ as a binary number, which results in 3.
